source_text: Ἀλλ’, ὡς ἔοικεν, ἔλαθον ὑπὸ φιλοτιμίας ἀποδεικτικῆς περαιτέρω τοῦ δέοντος παρεκβάς. ἐπιλείψει γάρ με ὁ βίος τὸ πλῆθος τῶν συμβολικῶς φιλοσοφούντων παρατιθέμενον. μνήμης τε οὖν ἕνεκεν καὶ συντομίας καὶ τοῦ πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀνατετάσθαι τοιαῦταί τινες αἱ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας γραφαί. τῶν γὰρ πολλάκις αὐταῖς πλησιαζόντων καὶ δοκιμασίαν δεδωκότων κατά τε τὴν πίστιν κατά τε τὸν βίον ἅπαντα μόνων ἐθέλουσιν ὑπάρχειν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν φιλοσοφίαν καὶ τὴν ἀληθῆ θεολογίαν. ναὶ μὴν ἐξηγητοῦ τινος καὶ καθηγητοῦ χρείαν ἔχειν ἡμᾶς βούλονται· οὕτως γὰρ καὶ σπουδασθήσεσθαι μᾶλλον καὶ ὠφελήσειν τοὺς ἀξίους αὐτῶν διελάμβανον καὶ ἀνεξαπατήτους τούτους ἔσεσθαι, παρὰ τῶν εὖ εἰδότων παραλαμβάνοντας. ἄλλως τε καὶ πάνθ’, ὅσα διά τινος παρακαλύμματος ὑποφαίνεται, μείζονά τε καὶ σεμνοτέραν δείκνυσι τὴν ἀλήθειαν. καθάπερ τὰ μὲν ὥρια διαφαίνοντα τοῦ ὕδατος, αἱ μορφαὶ δὲ διὰ τῶν παρακαλυμμάτων συνεμφάσεις τινὰς αὐταῖς προσχαριζομένων. ἐλεγκτικαὶ γὰρ αἱ περιαύγειαι πρὸς τῷ καὶ τὰ φανερὰ μονοτρόπως κατανοεῖσθαι. συνεκδοχὰς τοίνυν πλείονας ἐξὸν εἶναι λαμβάνειν, ὥσπερ οὖν λαμβάνομεν, ἐκ τῶν μετ’ ἐπικρύψεως εἰρημένων. ὧν οὕτως ἐχόντων σφάλλεται μὲν ὁ ἄπειρος καὶ ἀμαθής, καταλαμβάνει δὲ ὁ γνωστικός. ἤδη γοῦν οὐδὲ τοῖς τυχοῦσιν ἤθελον ἀνέδην ἐκκεῖσθαι πάντα, οὐδὲ κοινοποιεῖσθαι τὰ σοφίας ἀγαθὰ τοῖς μηδ’ ὄναρ τὴν ψυχὴν κεκαθαρμένοις· οὐ γὰρ θέμις ὀρέγειν τοῖς ἀπαντῶσι τὰ μετὰ τοσούτων ἀγώνων πορισθέντα οὐδὲ μὴν βεβήλοις τὰ τοῦ λόγου μυστήρια διηγεῖσθαι. φασὶ γοῦν Ἵππαρχον τὸν Πυθαγόρειον, αἰτίαν ἔχοντα γράψασθαι τὰ τοῦ Πυθαγόρου σαφῶς, ἐξελαθῆναι τῆς διατριβῆς καὶ στήλην ἐπ’ αὐτῷ γενέσθαι οἷα νεκρῷ. διὸ καὶ ἐν τῇ βαρβάρῳ φιλοσοφίᾳ νεκροὺς καλοῦσι τοὺς ἐκπεσόντας τῶν δογμάτων καὶ καθυποτάξαντας τὸν νοῦν τοῖς πάθεσι τοῖς ψυχικοῖς. τίς γὰρ μετοχὴ δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ἀνομίᾳ, κατὰ τὸν θεῖον ἀπόστολον, ἢ τίς κοινωνία φωτὶ πρὸς σκότος; τίς δὲ συμφώνησις Χριστοῦ πρὸς Βελίαρ; ἢ τίς μερὶς πιστῷ μετὰ ἀπίστου; δίχα γὰρ Ὀλυμπίων καὶ φθιμένων τιμαί. διὸ καὶ ἐξέρχεσθε ἐκ μέσου αὐτῶν καὶ ἀφορίσθητε, λέγει κύριος, καὶ ἀκαθάρτου μὴ ἅπτεσθε· κἀγὼ εἰσδέξομαι ὑμᾶς καὶ ἔσομαι ὑμῖν εἰς πατέρα, καὶ ὑμεῖς ἔσεσθέ μοι εἰς υἱοὺς καὶ θυγατέρας. Οὐ μόνοι ἄρα οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι καὶ Πλάτων τὰ πολλὰ ἐπεκρύπτοντο, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ Ἐπικούρειοί φασί τινα καὶ παρ’ αὐτοῦ ἀπόρρητα εἶναι καὶ μὴ πᾶσιν ἐπιτρέπειν ἐντυγχάνειν τούτοις τοῖς γράμμασιν. ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ Στωϊκοὶ λέγουσι Ζήνωνι τῷ πρώτῳ γεγράφθαι τινά, ἃ μὴ ῥᾳδίως ἐπιτρέπουσι τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἀναγινώσκειν, μὴ οὐχὶ πεῖραν δεδωκόσι πρότερον, εἰ γνησίως φιλοσοφοῖεν. λέγουσι δὲ καὶ οἱ Ἀριστοτέλους τὰ μὲν ἐσωτερικὰ εἶναι τῶν συγγραμμάτων αὐτοῦ, τὰ δὲ κοινά τε καὶ ἐξωτερικά. ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ τὰ μυστήρια θέμενοι, φιλόσοφοι ὄντες, τὰ αὑτῶν δόγματα τοῖς μύθοις κατέχωσαν, ὥστε μὴ εἶναι ἅπασι δῆλα· εἶθ’ οἳ μέν, ἀνθρωπίνας κατακρύψαντες δόξας, τοὺς ἀμαθεῖς ἐκώλυσαν ἐντυγχάνειν, τὴν δὲ τῶν ὄντων ὄντως ἁγίαν καὶ μακαρίαν θεωρίαν οὐ παντὸς μᾶλλον ἐπικεκρύφθαι συνέφερεν; πλὴν οὔτε τὰ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας οὔθ’ οἱ μῦθοι οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι, ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ οἱ παρὰ Πλάτωνι ἐν Πολιτείᾳ Ἠρὸς τοῦ Ἀρμενίου καὶ ἐν Γοργίᾳ Αἰακοῦ καὶ Ῥαδαμάνθυος καὶ ἐν Φαίδωνι ὁ τοῦ Ταρτάρου καὶ ἐν Πρωταγόρᾳ ὁ Προμηθέως καὶ Ἐπιμηθέως πρός τε τούτοις ὁ τοῦ πολέμου τῶν Ἀτλαντικῶν καὶ τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἐν τῷ Ἀτλαντικῷ, οὐχ ἁπλῶς κατὰ πάντα τὰ ὀνόματα ἀλληγορητέοι, ἀλλ’ ὅσα τῆς διανοίας τῆς καθόλου σημαντικά, καὶ δὴ ταῦτα ἐξεύροιμεν ἂν διὰ συμβόλων ὑπὸ παρακαλύμματι τῇ ἀλληγορίᾳ μηνυόμενα. Ναὶ μὴν καὶ ἡ Πυθαγόρου συνουσία καὶ ἡ πρὸς τοὺς ὁμιλητὰς διττὴ κοινωνία, ἀκουσματικοὺς τοὺς πολλοὺς καί τινας μαθηματικοὺς ἑτέρους καλοῦσα, τοὺς γνησίως ἀνθαπτομένους τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν φάσθαι, τὸ δὲ καὶ κεκρυμμένον εἶναι πρὸς τοὺς πολλοὺς ᾐνίσσετο. ἴσως δὲ καὶ τὸ διττὸν ἐκεῖνο εἶδος τῶν ἐκ τοῦ Περιπάτου, τὸ ἐν τοῖς λόγοις ἔνδοξόν τε καὶ ἐπιστημονικὸν καλούμενον, οὐκ ἀπήλλακται τοῦ διαιρεῖν δόξαν ἀπό τε εὐκλείας καὶ ἀληθείας. μηδέ σέ γ’ εὐδόξοιο βιήσεται ἄνθεα τιμῆς πρὸς θνητῶν ἀνελέσθαι, ἐφ’ ᾧ θ’ ὁσίης πλέον εἰπεῖν. αἱ γοῦν Ἰάδες μοῦσαι διαρρήδην λέγουσι τοὺς μὲν πολλοὺς καὶ δοκησισόφους δήμων ἀοιδοῖσιν ἕπεσθαι καὶ νόμοισι χρέεσθαι, εἰδότας ὅτι πολλοὶ κακοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἀγαθοί· τοὺς ἀρίστους δὲ τὸ κλέος μεταδιώκειν. αἱρεῦνται γάρ, φησίν, ἓν ἀντὶ πάντων οἱ ἄριστοι κλέος ἀέναον θνητῶν, οἱ δὲ πολλοὶ κεκόρηνται ὅπως κτήνεα, γαστρὶ καὶ αἰδοίοις καὶ τοῖς αἰσχίστοις τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν μετρήσαντες τὴν εὐδαιμονίαν· ὅ τ’ Ἐλεάτης Παρμενίδης ὁ μέγας διττῶν εἰσηγεῖται διδασκαλίαν ὁδῶν ὧδέ πως γράφων· ἠμὲν Ἀληθείης εὐπειθέος ἀτρεμὲς ἦτορ, ἠδὲ βροτῶν δόξας, ταῖς οὐκ ἔνι πίστις ἀληθής.
pass_a_gloss: But, as it seems, I have been concealed by a demonstrative ambition, having gone further than what is necessary. For my life will fail to recount the multitude of those philosophizing symbolically. Therefore, for the sake of memory, brevity, and being directed towards the truth, some writings of barbarian philosophy are such. For often those who approach them and have given a test, both in faith and in life, wish to possess only the true philosophy and the true theology. Indeed, they want us to have need of some interpreter and teacher; for thus they will be studied more and will benefit those worthy of them, taking and being unerring, receiving from those who know well. Besides, all things that are shown through some veil, show the truth as greater and more dignified. Just as the forms of water appear, but the shapes through veils bring some charm to them. For the surroundings are reproofs towards also understanding the visible things in a single way. Therefore, it is possible to take more interpretations, as we take them, from the things said with concealment. Of which, thus being, the inexperienced and ignorant person fails, but the knowledgeable person understands. Already, indeed, they did not want to pour out everything to those who happen upon it, nor to make common the good things of wisdom to those who have not even purified their soul in a dream; for it is not lawful to offer to those who encounter the things that have been acquired with so many struggles, nor to recount the mysteries of the Word to the profane. They say, indeed, that Hipparchus the Pythagorean, having written the things of Pythagoras clearly, was expelled from the school and a pillar was placed on him as on a dead person. Therefore, also in barbarian philosophy, they call those who have fallen away from the doctrines and have subjected their mind to the passions of the soul 'dead'. For what participation is there in righteousness and lawlessness, according to the divine apostle, or what communion is there between light and darkness? What harmony is there between Christ and Beliar? Or what part is there for the faithful with the unfaithful? For the honors are separate from the Olympic and the dead. Therefore, also come out from among them and be separated, says the Lord, and do not touch the unclean; and I will receive you and will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me. Not only, therefore, did the Pythagoreans and Plato conceal many things, but also the Epicureans say that some things are secret and not allowed to all to encounter these writings. But also the Stoics say that Zeno the first wrote some things that they do not easily allow the students to read, unless they have previously been tested, if they philosophize genuinely. They say, indeed, that the inner writings of Aristotle are different from the common and outer ones. But also those who establish the mysteries, being philosophers, hid their doctrines in myths, so that they would not be clear to all; then, having hidden human opinions, they prevented the ignorant from encountering them - was it not beneficial for the holy and blessed theory of what truly exists to be concealed from everyone? However, neither the things of barbarian philosophy nor the myths of Pythagoras, nor those in Plato's Politeia, nor the story of Er the Armenian, nor the story of Aiakos and Rhadamanthus in Gorgias, nor the story of Tartarus in Phaedo, nor the story of Prometheus and Epimetheus, nor the story of the war of the Atlantics and the Athenians in the Atlantic, are to be allegorized simply in all respects, but as much as the universal mind signifies, and we would find these things through symbols, veiled by allegory. Indeed, also the community of Pythagoras and the double communion with his companions, calling the many 'acousmatic' and some others 'mathematical', those who are genuinely kindled with philosophy, but what is said is one thing, and what is hidden is another, was hinted at to the many. Perhaps, also, that double kind of the Peripatetics, the one called noble and scientific in words, has not escaped dividing opinion from glory and truth. Nor will you, being glorious, seize the flowers of honor from mortals, on which one could say more about holiness. The Muses, indeed, say openly that the many and the pretended philosophers follow the poets of the people and use their laws, knowing that many are evil, but few are good; the best are pursued by fame. For they choose, he says, one thing instead of all, eternal fame among mortals, but the many are satisfied like cattle, measuring happiness by the belly and the shameful things in us; as also the great Eleatic Parmenides introduces a double teaching of ways, writing thus: 'on the one hand, the unshakeable heart of persuasive Truth, on the other hand, the opinions of mortals, in which there is no true faith'.

pass_b_english: It appears I have been led astray by a demonstrative ambition, carrying my argument further than necessity demands. My life would fall short if I tried to catalog every thinker who philosophizes through symbols. So, for the sake of memory, brevity, and keeping our course set toward the truth, I present these writings of barbarian philosophy. Those who frequently draw near to them and have proven themselves in both faith and life desire to possess nothing less than the true philosophy and the true theology. They insist that we require an interpreter and a guide; only then will these writings be studied with proper diligence, benefit those worthy of them, and remain uncorrupted, received from those who know them well. Besides, anything glimpsed through a veil displays the truth as greater and more dignified—just as the forms of water appear clearly, but shapes seen through coverings gain an added charm. Such veils serve as checks, compelling us to understand visible realities in a unified way. Consequently, we can and do draw multiple interpretations from statements made under concealment. The inexperienced and ignorant stumble over these; the knowledgeable grasp them.

From the outset, the authors did not wish to pour everything out indiscriminately, nor to make the goods of wisdom common property for those who have not even purified their souls in a dream. It is not lawful to offer what was won through such great struggles to every chance comer, nor to recount the mysteries of the Word to the profane. They tell of Hipparchus the Pythagorean, who was expelled from the school and marked with a pillar as if dead because he wrote Pythagoras's teachings plainly. So too in barbarian philosophy, those who fall away from the doctrines and subject their minds to the passions of the soul are called 'dead.' For what partnership can righteousness have with lawlessness, according to the divine apostle, or what communion can light have with darkness? What harmony exists between Christ and Beliar? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? Honors belong to the Olympians, not to the dead. Therefore, "Come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and do not touch the unclean; and I will welcome you, and I will be a father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters" (2 Corinthians 6:17; 2 Corinthians 6:18).

It was not only the Pythagoreans and Plato who concealed much. The Epicureans also claim that some teachings are secret and not permitted to all. The Stoics say that Zeno, their founder, wrote certain things they do not readily allow students to read unless they have first been tested to see if they philosophize genuinely. Aristotle's followers distinguish his inner writings from those that are common and exoteric. Even the philosophers who established the mysteries hid their doctrines in myths so they would not be clear to everyone; having concealed mere human opinions, they kept the ignorant from access—was it not beneficial that the holy and blessed contemplation of true being should be veiled from all? Yet neither the contents of barbarian philosophy, nor the Pythagorean myths, nor those in Plato's Republic—the myth of Er the Armenian, the judgment of Aeacus and Rhadamanthus in the Gorgias, the tale of Tartarus in the Phaedo, the story of Prometheus and Epimetheus in the Protagoras, and the war of the Atlanteans and Athenians in the Atlantic—are to be allegorized simply in every detail. Only insofar as they signify something universal to the mind should they be so read; these are the things we would discover through symbols veiled by allegory.

Indeed, Pythagoras's own community practiced a twofold fellowship with his companions: he called the many 'acousmatics' and a few others 'mathematicians,' those genuinely kindled by philosophy. But the distinction between what is said openly and what is kept hidden from the many was itself hinted at. Perhaps, too, that twofold division among the Peripatetics—the teachings called 'noble' and 'scientific'—has not escaped the separation of reputation from truth. Nor will you, glorious one, seize the flowers of honor from mortals, a subject on which more could be said concerning holiness. The Muses declare plainly that the many and the pretended sophists follow the poets of the people and use their laws, knowing that the wicked are many and the good few; the best pursue glory. "For they choose," he says, "one thing instead of all: eternal fame among mortals. But the many are satisfied like cattle, measuring happiness by the belly, the genitals, and the basest parts within us." The great Eleatic Parmenides also sets forth a twofold teaching of ways, writing thus: "On the one hand, the unshakeable heart of persuasive Truth; on the other, the opinions of mortals, in which there is no true faith."

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex allegorical discussions and the distinctions between different philosophical schools. Scripture citations (2 Corinthians 6:17; 2 Corinthians 6:18) are correctly added to the quoted text in Pass B. The translation of the Parmenides fragment at the end is faithful to the Greek. All clauses in the Greek are accounted for in both Pass A and Pass B.
